title: Nobody Independently Knows How People Actually Use AI
hook: Almost everything we 'know' about how people use chatbots comes from the companies selling them — and they publish only the slices they choose.
key_points: OpenAI and Anthropic regularly publish usage reports on ChatGPT and Claude, MIT Technology Review notes.
Researchers say there's no independent source to corroborate any of it.
Stanford's Anka Reuel: 'There is no independent source to corroborate it.'
The companies control what's measured, how it's grouped, and what stays unpublished.
Those same reports get cited in policy debates and news coverage as if they were neutral statistics.
Read vendor usage data as marketing-adjacent evidence, not as a census.
content_html: Anthropic and OpenAI both publish reports on how people use Claude and ChatGPT — the kind of documents that become headlines about what AI is doing to work, school, and daily life. AI researchers speaking to MIT Technology Review make a simple point about all of them: nobody can check the numbers. "There is no independent source to corroborate it," says Anka Reuel, a computer science PhD candidate at Stanford.
extra_html:
The companies decide what to measure, how to categorize it, which slices to publish, and which to leave out. None of that requires bad faith to produce a distorted picture — it's just what happens when the only party with the data is also the party with something to sell.

The habit worth building: when you see a claim about how "people" use AI, ask who did the counting. Vendor telemetry is real evidence, and it's often the best available, but it isn't a census — and treating it as one has already shaped news coverage and policy arguments. Eileen Guo's piece for MIT Technology Review walks through what independent researchers would need instead.

related.title: Hype or Real?
related.hook: AI coverage swings between 'this changes everything' and 'it's all a bubble.' The truth is usually in between — and a few questions help you judge any big AI claim for yourself.

related.title: Half of Americans Use Chatbots — Most Think AI Is Moving Too Fast
related.hook: A new Pew poll captures the mood of the AI era: chatbot use has jumped to about half of Americans, yet nearly two-thirds say the technology is advancing too quickly.

related.title: Your Data & Privacy
related.hook: When you type into a free AI tool, you might be the product. What you share can be stored, reviewed by humans, and used to train future models — so share like it's not private.

flashcards.prompt: What's the core problem with company-published AI usage reports?

choices.text: There's no independent source to corroborate them — the vendor picks what to measure and release
They are illegal to publish in most countries
They are always written by outside auditors

flashcards.explanation_html: Researchers quoted by MIT Technology Review point out the data can't be checked against anything else, and the companies choose which slices to make public.

flashcards.prompt: Why does this gap matter outside of academia?
flashcards.back_html: These reports get cited in journalism and policy debates as if they were neutral statistics about society, when they're self-selected vendor data.

flashcards.prompt: How should you read a headline like 'most people use AI for X'?
flashcards.back_html: Ask who counted. If the number comes from the company selling the product, treat it as evidence with an interest attached, not as a measurement of the population.
